catalog_quote: Mamaindê stress is first of all conditioned by morphology. When the Mamaindê word is looked at as an unanalyzable sequence, stress is impossible to predict. ... Primary stress occurs on the root morpheme alone, while secondary stress can occur both in the root and in the affix classes closest to the root. The affixes that occur in strata/morpheme classes furthest from the root never get stressed, even if their syllable structure would make them candidates for stress. ... This time the pattern is clear. Mamaindê presents a quantity sensitive stress system, in which stress is assigned to every heavy syllable in the root. Primary stress is on the rightmost of the heavy syllables. In cases where there are no heavy syllables within the root, and quantity cannot play its stress-attracting role, primary stress is still right-headed, being located on the right-most light syllable. ... [p.146] S…
sweep_summary: Mamaindé (mama1278) is in the catalog as weight-sensitive, deciding source Eberhard 2009 (LOT 236, held on file and re-read this sweep at pp.140-145; quote verbatim). The three sweep items are the author's 1993 UTA MA thesis, its 1995 SIL/UTA PL 122 book version, and Stonham's 1998 review of it in Word 49(1):134-141. None could be read: the 1993 thesis has no open copy (UTA repository Cloudflare-blocked); the 1995 book is search-only on HathiTrust (2 copies) and SIL Global's site is Cloudflare-blocked from our machine; Stonham 1998 sits inside the paywalled T&F 'Reviews' bundle DOI 10.1080/00437956.1998.11673880. Two further reviews of the 1995 book were found via Crossref: Kenstowicz 1996 (Phonology 13(3):450-455, DOI 10.1017/s0952675700002748) and Price 1996 (IJAL 62(3):314-316, DOI 10.1086/466300). The publisher's first-page preview of Kenstowicz was fetched sources and scanned (p.450): it reports the 1995 analysis as closed-syllable weight attracting stress, some closed affix syllables systematically unstressed, and primary stress always on a stem syllable, which confirms the catalog coding. Eberhard 2009 states (p.140, fn.138) that its basic conclusions equal the 1995 monograph with 'a few crucial differences', so the 2009 grammar remains the best statement and nothing found supersedes it. All items are low/none acquisition priority; everything fetched sources is under with. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Google Books API, scholar.archive and DuckDuckGo were rate-limited or refused.

new_statements.reading: Word stress is computed over the root (stem), not the whole word: every heavy syllable of the root is stressed, primary stress falls on the rightmost heavy syllable of the root, and if the root has no heavy syllable primary stress falls on the root-final (rightmost light) syllable; affixes get at most secondary stress (inner classes, heavy syllables only) and outer affixes never any. Weight-sensitive, right-headed, morphologically bounded. This is the same text the catalog already quotes; the sweep produced nothing that outranks it, and Kenstowicz's 1996 review (p.450, read) independently reports the same weight/stem-based pattern for the 1995 analysis that the 2009 grammar explicitly updates.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim in the held LOT 236 PDF/txt at pp.144-145, 146, 151, 152-153; domain quote p.175 confirmed. (2) Deciding source: a 608-pp 2009 reference grammar (published PhD) whose stress chapter is by the same fieldworker who wrote the language's only stress monograph (1995) and which explicitly updates that monograph; it is the top item in Glottolog's descriptive list and the best available description of Mamaindê stress. The coding (weight-sensitive, CVV+CVC heavy, unbounded rightmost-heavy-else-final over the root domain, outer strata unstressable) matches the source's prose (pp.144-145) and formal rules (QS, ERFF, ERFW, pp.146-157). The recorded 14/20 example fit is not a sourcing defect: the six misses are the source's own 'apparent exceptions' (sect. 2.3.5.7, lexical post-stress vowels in i-class nouns/a-class verbs, p.182 'Attempts to predict when these post-stres

sources.quote: Things become a little clearer when weight is factored in: closed syllables are heavy and attract stress while open light syllables are skipped (see below); however, some closed syllables remain systematically unstressed: e.g. the third syllable in wanun-ax-wa 'I am good' and the second in wa-nunta-wa 'you obviously will come'. ... The various Mamaindé stress patterns begin to make sense once the morphology is taken into account. First (putting aside a single exception; see below), one of the syllables of the stem always bears a primary stress: e.g. walekhan-txu 'chief (INDEF)', hala-txu 'land (INDEF)', wet-txu 'child (INDEF)'.
sources.note: Independent metrical phonologist's reading of the same system (cited by Eberhard 2009 fn.138 as 'a helpful review'); useful third-party check on the QS-unbounded/right-headed analysis and on whether foot-level marks count as secondary stress.
